newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say time on their side in hostage saga.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say time on their side in hostage saga.

text.p: A leader of Marxist guerrillas holding 72 people hostage in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima said time was on the rebels' side in the 10-week-old standoff as talks entered a lull on Wednesday.
In an interview at a secret jungle location, he said the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) was prepared to wait as long as necessary for a "dignified" solution to the siege.

"We are in no hurry. We have time on our side," the man who identified himself as "Comrade Alejandro," a member of the MRTA's high command, said in his second meeting with Reuters at a rebel training camp in Central Peru.
"What do we lose if we wait months, when we have waited centuries for a revolution?"

He said the start of negotiations last week between the government and Nestor Cerpa, leader of the guerrillas who seized the Japanese residence on Dec. 17, showed the government was "starting to give ground."

But President Alberto Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, also claims "Oriental" patience to see through the crisis, already the longest of its sort in Latin America's history. Fujimori has made no sign of shifting his position and continues to reject the MRTA's main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.

The MRTA said last week for the first time it may drop its insistence that all of the rebels be freed and negotiate for the release of a smaller number, depending on their experience or importance in the movement.

"We hope there is an accord that benefits both sides," Alejandro said, adding the MRTA would be satisfied only with a "dignified" solution to the siege. Such a solution would mean either a bloody end where Peruvian security forces stormed the fortified compound or, in the case of a peaceful outcome, one where "the morale of the movement remained high," he added.

After a series of recent meetings, the government and hostage-takers have agreed to pause until Thursday before restarting negotiations. There were no details given of Tuesday's discussions -- the sixth round -- but Peruvian and Japanese officials were upbeat about progress in the talks.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto told reporters on Wednesday: "As with the previous session, it seems to have been conducted in a very good atmosphere. They may be starting work to sort out points of agreement and differences."
If the MRTA did win the release of its jailed comrades, the movement's leader, Victor Polay, would not take up arms again and would work instead for a lasting peace, his mother said.

"If my son should get out of prison, he would feel an urgent need to rejoin his family," Otilia Campos de Polay told Reuters. "I do not think he would reorganize the movement because now he is 44 and not the impetuous young man who founded the MRTA when he was 28."
